newsitem.title: USA: U.S. help needed for Mideast Peace - Netanyahu.
newsitem.headline: U.S. help needed for Mideast Peace - Netanyahu.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu feels U.S. help will be needed to achieve peace with the Palestinians, but it is he and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat who must face their constituencies at the end of the process, Newsweek magazine reported on Sunday.
Arafat must tell his people that they cannot realise all their goals, Netanyahu told Newsweek.
In an interview with the magazine, Netanhahu also:
-- said he favours accelerated peace talks.
-- refused to stop housing construction in Jerusalem.
-- refused to give up any Israeli settlements.
"I can't envision reaching a final settlement with the Palestinians without continuous American assistance," he told the magazine.

But, he said, "at the end of the day, it is Israel and the Palestinians, Arafat and myself, who will have to face our constituencies. I have made a very difficult and long journey -- having accepted the Oslo accords before the elections and having lived with their provisions. What is required now is a similar determination by the Palestinians. Arafat must face his people and say: 'We cannot get all that we want'."

"I have no desire to subjugate the Palestinian population," the prime minister said of a Palestinian state. "Right now, 99 percent of them are under Palestinian civil control and I envision that they will pass to Palestinian self-government. But equally, I believe that the granting of unlimited self-determination would mean that we would face a Palestinian army with heavy weapons, a state that could make military pacts with countries like Iran or Iraq...."

In answer to a question of whether he was willing to suspend building of the Har Homa development in Jerusalem, Netanyahu said that "under the Oslo agreements, Israel has complete freedom to build in Jerusalem."

"We must move to accelerated talks for the completion of the final-status agreements," Netanyahu told Newsweek. "If we engage in a slow, step-by-step process, we will erode confidence; a package approach has a greater chance of success."
Netanyahu has offered to cede more than 40 percent of the West Bank to Palestinians; he told the magazine he wanted to keep "a united Jerusalem and its immediate environs and the Jordan valley."
"We're not in the business of uprooting populations, Arab or Jewish," Netanyahu replied when asked whether Israel would give up settlements.
